title: Dropping Fear
speaker: Ninen Susan Elbe
summary: Ninen Susan Elbe's talk explores how fear can be a habitual pattern that affects our relationships and well-being, but also offers a way out of it by cultivating confidence and faith in ourselves and others. By letting go of preconceived notions and embracing the present moment, we can experience life more fully and connect with others on a deeper level. This involves practicing generosity, compassion, and vulnerability, which allows us to find moments of repose and connection with the world around us.

I was Shuso, Norman Fischer Shuso, in 2009 and ordained as a priest in 2016.
In the past I've been able to spend a lot of time down in Bellingham and meet a lot of Bellingham practitioners, and I've become friends with many of you.
So it's absolutely wonderful to be here with you, to talk and to share this with you.
My actual preference would be to take everybody off mute and just chat and forget about my talk, but I don't think that's part of the program.
So I'd better get started and give you a little talk and see how it goes.
Excuse me.
First of all, I want to let you know that at this moment I'm sitting just south of the city of Vancouver proper, in a place called Tsawwassen.
It's the traditional territory of the Tsawwassen First Nations people, who have been the stewards of this beautiful area.
I would like to express my gratitude to them and my wishes for peace, healing and happiness.
As I mentioned, Mountain Rain and Red Cedar used to practice together a lot, and we would visit each other's sanghas north and south of the border.
I really hope that one day soon we can all practice together again in person.
But for now we have our shared intention, which is amazingly powerful, because we've been able to do this over Zoom for almost a year now.
And we have advanced technology.
So thank you for tuning in today and for listening to my talk.
I told Chris that the title of my talk would be something about dropping fear.
Why did I want to talk about fear?
It doesn't sound like such a Zen topic.
After all, when have you ever heard or read a Zen teacher who said, "Be cautious," or "Defend and protect your territory," or "Don't look stupid," or "Watch out for others"?
It's just not something you hear.
And yet I think it's a very Zen topic, because in a sense fear is probably the most basic reason why we practice.
It's the connection and cause of a lot of our suffering.
When Chris called me up a few weeks ago and asked if I would give a talk, some of my first thoughts were, "Oh, gee, I don't know what I would talk about.
There are so many other great learned and wise teachers in our two sanghas and beyond.
Who am I to say anything?
I don't know."
After a moment I realized this was my ever loud and noisy imposter syndrome popping up, which is a kind of first line of self-defense, a first response.
Rather than having the first thought be, "Hey, my friend Chris wants a bit of help.
Perhaps I could offer something," it was, "No, no, no."
Or maybe I could have thought, "Well, Norman Fischer invited me to be a Shuso in 2009, so he must have thought I was a safe choice to talk to others about Dharma."
No, I went straight to fear.
Fear is an attitude towards life that some, if not all of us, carry around like pretty heavy chains.
It's the part of us that feels like tightness, holding back, self-protection and defensiveness.
The result of carrying around this attitude is that it becomes a habit.
We end up saying things that may be less than kind and doing things that are questionable, that can mess with our relationships and ultimately our health and state of mind.
At the base of it, it reinforces our sense of self as separate from others, and that sounds just like what the Buddha came into this world to cure.
So after a moment of talking to Chris, I gently put aside my imposter syndrome and this fear about who am I to talk.
There are no guarantees that I won't come across as an imposter or that I will be able to give you a scintillating talk,
but I will try, because somebody might find it helpful, entertaining or just a good break from sitting.
I thought I could explore what has been topmost in my mind and on my heart over the last few months.
Combined with what I've been studying in the last while, I thought I could cobble something together.
In this talk, I'll try to share what I've learned about the way fear informs how we are in the world, and what some other teachers have thought about it.
I also hope I can encourage you to investigate how fear manifests in your life and your practice, and ways that you might expand your perspective on fear.
To do this, I'll talk about my experience, which I already have, and parts of the Sandokai,
which is one of my most recent studies, and how it helped open this topic for me.
So it's going to be a bit of a mash-up, but I thought I'd give it a try.
In the autumn, Mountain Rain Zen held its practice period.
We studied the Paramitas, or the six perfections, that define the path of a Bodhisattva, the path to compassion and awakening.
As part of my practice period study, I took another look at Norman Fischer's book called The World Could Be Otherwise.
In his book, Norman describes the Paramitas from his particular point of view.
I was deeply touched by the first chapter in his book,
which was on the Paramita of generosity.
As I reread this chapter, it struck me that a big part of my experience over many years of Zen has been how the grip of fear has been loosened in me because of the generosity I've received.
Norman describes the traditional Buddhist view of generosity as having three parts.
First, material: actual physical or material gifts.
Second, spiritual: teaching or inspiration.
And finally, fearlessness.
I found the aspect of fearlessness as a component of generosity kind of amazing,
as I hadn't seen it that way before.
Although when I heard this, I knew from my own experience that it was, without a doubt, true, and perhaps nowhere more than in my Buddhist practice.
So how does one give a gift of fearlessness?
Norman says you give it by giving love, because when you feel loved, you feel confident.
To give the gift of fearlessness is to give others the sense that they matter, that they are respected, cared for, secure within a loving reality, and therefore ultimately protected.
How many times have I come away from Dokusan with one of my teachers feeling this way,
even if not many words were said, or even if I thought the words were unsatisfactory?
There's something else that comes out of the Dokusan meeting room for me sometimes, and it's larger.
It's larger than both of us.
And it's, I think, in large part a dropping or a release of this fear.
I've felt this spaciousness and great safety in being able to express whatever was coming up in my life and practice.
As for why a bodhisattva gives fearlessness, it is because they, in another quote from Norman here, have genuine confidence that there really is nothing to fear,
because love is actually built into the order of reality.
Knowing that reality is inherently generous and loving certainly doesn't mean that bad things can't happen.
Shame, loss, physical pain, and even death are part of life.
They are folded into the bodhisattva's imaginative vision of the path ahead.
Everything that exists will one day not exist.
This is how existence works.
This is its beauty and the source of its bounty.
Following our practice period at Mountain Rain and the study of the Paramitas,
I studied the Sandokai, which, because of the state of my heart or mind, became focused through this lens on the Paramita of generosity.
The Sandokai was a favorite of Shunryu Suzuki's, and we may know it as the harmony of difference and equality.
I read Suzuki's thoughts in the book Branching Streams Flow in the Darkness.
It is often chanted in Zen centers, and I know Red Cedar has this in its chant book.
It's been revised a little bit since Shunryu Suzuki put it in his book, and maybe Telus can launch it for us in a screen share.
Are you able to do that, Telus?
*The mind of the great sage of India is intimately transmitted from west to east.
While human faculties are sharp or dull, the way has no northern or southern ancestors.
The spiritual source shines clear in the light.
The branching streams flow on in the dark.*
*Grasping at things is surely delusion.
According with sameness is still not enlightenment.
All the objects of the senses interact and yet do not.
Interacting brings involvement.
Otherwise, each keeps its place.
Sites vary in quality and form.
Sounds differ as pleasing or harsh.
Refined and common speech come together in the dark.*
*Clear and murky phrases are distinguished in the light.
The four elements return to their natures just as a child turns to its mother.
Fire heats, wind moves, water wets, earth is solid, eye and sight, ear and sound, nose and smell, tongue and taste, thus for each and every thing, depending on these roots, the leaves spread forth.
Trunk and branches share the essence.
Revered and common each has its speech.
In the light there is darkness, but don't take it as darkness.*
*In the dark there is light, but don't see it as light.
Light and dark oppose one another, like the front and back foot in walking.
Each of the myriad things has its merit, expressed according to function and place.
Phenomena exist, like box and lid joining.
Principle accords, like arrow points meeting.
Hearing the words, understand the meaning.
Don't set up standards of your own.
If you don't understand the way right before you, how will you know the path as you walk?*
*Practice is not a matter of far or near, but if you are confused, mountains and rivers block your way.
I respectfully urge you who study the mystery, do not pass your days and nights in vain.*
This sutra was written by our Zen ancestor, named Sekito Kisen in Japanese or Shitou Xiqian, if I'm saying that correctly, in Chinese.
He was born in southern China in the Guangdong province and lived between the years 700 and 790 of the common era.
I've always found it to be a really beautiful poem, and that's how I appreciated it for a long time, for the beauty of its words and the images it evoked.
However, there's a lot more in it, and I won't be able to describe it or really talk about it all today.
I'll only explore the one aspect that I'm talking about today.
At its heart, aside from the references to Zen history and the Zen schools in China, this sutra describes the intimate connection of everything in the world.
Some might describe this as the complete interpenetration of the relative and absolute, or non-duality, or non-separation.
And I believe the more we can really absorb and manifest this understanding of non-separation or non-duality, the more fear will lessen its grip on us.

One way I think of the absolute, which can be a difficult term to wrap your head around, is the realm where things simply exist, or where events occur completely whole within each moment before our human individual minds assign meaning and value to them.
I think that realm is described in the lines, "Phenomena exist like box and cover joining, principal accords like arrow points meeting."
These lines remind me of how a First Nations wooden blanket box seals so tightly when you put the lid on that you almost don't think there is a separate lid and box.
The other thing it reminds me of is Mahakasyapa's enlightenment, when the Buddha holds up a flower and smiles.
Mahakasyapa smiles back.
Nothing else is needed.
To me, this is the complete meeting of each moment.
It's the mind before it engages and develops interpretations about whatever it has experienced.
It's a recognition of each moment as complete, like arrow points meeting in midair.
That sharp, definite, exact meeting without the confusion of karma or interpretation or all of the feelings about things that usually intrude on our experience of the world.
Each individual has a role in co-creating the entire world that surrounds us and runs through us: the air we breathe, the water we drink, the earth we walk on, the food we eat.
We all support ourselves and everyone else in an independent network.
Or on a more simple plane, you could think of the example of when you hear a voice.
It involves vocal cords, vibration, air, sound waves, eardrums, and a listener or receiver.
Each of these things exists in its own moment, a thing unto itself.
But none of it takes on any meaning until all of these are brought together in our human perceptions.
But how often is it that we only perceive before we think good or bad or indifferent about something we perceive?

I'm not quite sure how neuroscientists take these measurements, but they've found that there are mere milliseconds between the time a sensation is received and our minds react in some way with that good or bad or indifferent.
Our mind's assignment of a value is a natural human activity because we do, in fact, exist in the world as individuals.
We live in a relative world, and it allows us to practice.
The functioning of our minds allows us to make sense of the world, to piece things together, and to evaluate whether something will support or endanger our continued existence.
It has a very practical function.
We'd miss the words that are spoken by a voice if we just existed in the absolute.
We'd only experience, moment by moment, each element of sound and hearing and vocal cords and sound waves as completely independent things.
But the next lines in the Sandokai recognize that this interpretation can go a bit far.
And those lines are:
*Hearing the words, understand the meaning, don't set up standards on your own.*
I think Shunryu Suzuki is talking about this in his book in chapter 11, which is titled "We should not stick to words or rules too much."
This title alone reminds me of how we can get confused when we always look for things to be black and white, when there are so many shades of grey.
We box ourselves into a certain way of being, a certain way of acting.
We can't see our way out of that situation.

Maybe all we have in our toolbox, so to speak, are some principles that we've received through our experience or heard about, or maybe even those unspoken guidelines, those social mores that are implicit in our actions.
When we operate our lives that way, trying to pigeonhole everything into shapes we already know, we miss the potential for what could be.
And it can be scary to do otherwise.
But by doing this, we also take away our own freedom, because we choose to act only out of a received worldview of certain things, where they're either right or wrong, and there's nothing in between.
We can completely miss the middle path or the way through a challenging situation.
The next line in the sutra:
*If you don't understand the path as it meets your eyes, how can you know the way as you walk?*
Reminds me of someone being lost in a large city.
You try to figure out which way is west or east, but you're just going by a route you took when you visited the city many years ago.
Since then, a whole bunch of bridges and overpasses and traffic circles have been built.

It's frustrating because you try to rely on your past understanding, comparing it with a similar situation that you experienced before or your faulty memory of how the city was when you visited it many years ago.
So you need to find a different tool, a different way of looking and a different way of seeing.
I guess practically you just turn on Google Maps on your phone if you have that.
The next line:
*Progress is not a matter of far or near, but if you are confused, mountains and rivers block the way.*
I think what this line is telling me is that sometimes we have to let go of a goal in order to make progress.
The goal can get in the way if we have a preconceived notion of what it is we're supposed to attain or obtain.
It reminds me of the walks that I take during my coffee breaks.
I don't really drink coffee that often, but I do take breaks, especially when I'm working from home, which is what I do all the time these days.
So I head out of my back door, having faith that I'll make my way home because I'm familiar with my neighbourhood.
It allows me, while walking, to enjoy each step, legs and arms swinging, the smell of recent rainfall or things growing, the sounds of different birds.
I'm not thinking about getting home, and quite often, not really anything at all.
If I'm lucky, my shoulders drop and my neck relaxes.
Of course, I might be a little bit more cautious, and it might be a little bit more frightening, if not unwise, to completely forget the goal if I'm out in a wilderness forest.
In that case, I might sort of space the moments between my goal and my destination a little bit closer.
But if I'm constantly worried about that goal, I'll probably miss a lot of the experience.
The final line in the sutra is:
*I humbly say to those who study the mystery, don't waste time.*
One way that I interpret this is that if we're always trying to engage our analytical mind, grab on to something, like, "I've got to understand this.
This is too confusing.
I have to know what this is about," we miss a lot.
The tendency to be over-analytical is, we mainly engage our past way of understanding or doing things, in other words, our karma.
We say, "Oh, I figured this out a certain way in the past, and it worked."
I'm sure you know from experience that this is not always going to work.
It's only by responding to the moment as it arises that we can avoid being caught in our past and caught in our karma.
By studying the mystery, we're also bringing in, and when I say studying the mystery, it's like studying the mystery.
Maybe you're bringing to bear every one of the past sutras you've chanted or Dharma books that you've read.
This is great, but it doesn't allow you to experience the wonder of one particular moment at one particular time.
If you're Mahakasyapa, you'd see the flower and go, "Oh yeah, that's nice.
I've got another one."
It's our human shorthand, this way of the mind interpreting things, reacting.
Things arise so quickly that this relative body and this relative mind has to interpret and make sense of things to ensure our survival and to go forward in life.
We reinforce a sense of self as separate from everything else.
More and more we begin to see things only as they relate to ourselves, to our sense of security, to our sense of well-being.
Is this good for me?
Do I want this?
Do I like this?
Do I want to avoid it?
At their most basic, these reactions are desire and aversion, which the Buddha identified as the source of suffering.
We suffer in part because we can never find that perfect state of ease, neither running towards nor running away from things.
We lose touch with the interdependent nature of everything, the possibility that there is in the shades of grey.
This also makes it difficult for compassion to simply flow forth.
Something as natural as Diao Wu's reaching back for the pillow at night, as he describes to Yun Yang.
It's a natural action, where the hand doesn't tell your sore neck, "Don't bug me, I'm busy sleeping."
The hand is, of course, quite separate from the neck.
And there isn't some big dialogue that takes place between the two.
This is a spontaneous action of one part helping the other.
But we don't see our lives so much as the unplanned action of the hand that's going to fluff the pillow to make the neck more comfortable.
We do, in fact, think about how, "Oh, if I do this thing, I may not be well-rested for work tomorrow.
If I'm not well-rested for work, I'm going to mess up."
Do you hear the common word there?
It's the word "I."
It's the fear that's arising more and more as we separate ourselves from everything else.
It's the self-concept that arises and gets reinforced as thoughts, based in fear, feed on themselves if you let them.
It becomes a self-sustaining loop where the focus is the reinforcement of the strong sense of self and sense of separation.
The antidote, I think there are a number of different ways that we can loosen the grip of fear.
It's in Zazen, where we can find moments of repose and a tiny bit of extra space between perception and reaction.
Instead of reacting, maybe we can respond out of the grounding of the paramitas, out of the grounding of the precepts.

Another method of practice is by exercising patience and understanding in sangha practice, by bringing harmony rather than conflict to situations, by meeting our teachers in dokusan where we can truly experience being heard.
Or we can practice non-judgmental listening with others.
By applying the lessons we learn in the paramita of generosity, by letting go of our defended natures, judgments, caution, second-guessing, and demand for black and white answers.
It is a practice of being vulnerable, of launching ourselves into what we don't know with the intention and maybe even effect of reducing or ending suffering.
Norman quotes some lines from the Prajnaparamita Sutra in 8,000 Lines that describe this brave practice of letting go of the self-concept and practicing generosity.
Norman goes on to say that these lines acknowledge fear as an essential ingredient in our personalities.
He adds:
*We identify fear as an essential ingredient in our personalities.
We identify fear as an essential ingredient.*
He adds:
*We identify with the vulnerable self.
We think we are and possess what we are not and do not possess.
Hence, fear and loss of self and possessions is essential in us.*

At the end of his chapter on the paramita of generosity, Norman in his wise way offers some simple and practical suggestions of generosity and to help us find a greater sense of connection with the world.
So I'll just mention a few of my favorites here.
*Wipe the counters in public restrooms and recall that you do this for the next person coming in and for the counter itself.
Intentionally smile at people, anyone and everyone.
Try to feel the inner warmth that the smile outwardly projects.
Do something every day for your own health and well-being.
Meditate, exercise, eat a healthy diet.
Give the gift of fearlessness.
It's difficult but it's worthwhile.
Try it again and again.
Look at people with the eyes of love, respect, and genuine concern.
And try to find those feelings within yourself.*
And I'll just conclude with some of Eihei Dogen's words on generosity from the Bodhisattva's Four Methods of Guidance in the Shobogenzo.
*Know that to give to yourself is a part of giving.
To give to your family is also giving.
Even when you give a particle of dust, you should rejoice in your own act because you authentically transmit the merit of all Buddhas and begin to practice an act of a Bodhisattva.
The mind of a sentient being is difficult to change.
Mind is beyond measure.
Things given are beyond measure.
And yet, in giving, mind transforms the gift and the gift transforms the mind.*
Thank you so much for listening, and please stay safe, stay healthy, and stay well.
